background.definition: Pityriasis alba is a common, benign, recurrent, self-limited skin condition in school-age children characterized by irregular hypopigmented patches and macules with fine scale along sun-exposed skin of the face, extremities, and upper body.

list.listitem: The disease occurs in about 5% of children, with a range of 1-25% depending on the location of the study.
The etiology of pityriasis alba is unknown.
Pityriasis alba more commonly affects children with history of atopy, but it can also affect nonatopic individuals.

The condition has been associated with darker skin phototype and sun exposure, especially when sunscreen is not used. Affected areas are accentuated by the tanning or darkening of normal perilesional skin.
The disease is also associated with increased frequency of baths (≥2 per day) and hot water baths.

Some studies show association with intestinal parasites, zinc deficiency, copper deficiency, and iron deficiency anemia; the significance of these findings and their relationship to pityriasis alba are uncertain.

Microscopic features of pityriasis alba are consistent with a mild dermatitis with associated decreased melanin production. It is suspected that areas of eczema lead to decreased local melanin production.

This is especially apparent in darker-skinned individuals because they tend to tan easily, except in localized areas of eczema with decreased melanin production. The hypopigmentation and scaly patches are more apparent on areas of the skin with the most sun exposure (eg, the face).
Reduction of sun exposure, regular use of sunscreen, and decreased frequency (<2 per day) and temperature of baths (lukewarm rather than hot) may decrease the recurrence of pityriasis alba. C
Suspect pityriasis alba in atopic school-age children presenting with irregular hypopigmented patches and macules with fine scale of the face and extremities, accentuated by sun exposure. C

In cases of clinical uncertainty, perform potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings to differentiate pityriasis alba from tinea versicolor, which may show "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance of Malassezia yeast. C

Differential.Differential_Features: KOH prep may reveal "spaghetti (pseudohyphae) and meatballs (spores)" appearance of Malassezia yeast.

list.listitem: Pityriasis alba common affects school-age children (ages 3-16) and can present in different stages.
Early disease may present as erythematous patches with raised edges, lasting several weeks. Erythema subsequently subsides, leaving smooth scale.
Patients generally present to clinic during the later stage of the disease, with clearly defined, somewhat irregular, hypopigmented patches and macules with fine scale at the edges.
Lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic.
Pityriasis alba typically occurs in sun-exposed areas such as the face (cheeks, forehead), neck, upper trunk, and extremities.
Lesions are more apparent in the summer months when the surrounding skin tans. They may resolve during winter, but may relapse during the summer.

The hypopigmented patches typically resolve between 6 months to 7 years. In atopic children, hypopigmentation may take longer to disappear, but spontaneous resolution generally occurs prior to adulthood.
There are no routine diagnostic tests.
A negative KOH prep is helpful to rule out tinea versicolor.

On dermoscopic examination, pityriasis alba may appear as poorly demarcated white macules with fine scales. Hairs inside the lesions appear normal in color. Occasionally, erythema is observed inside and outside the hypopigmented macules.
See algorithm in for the approach to the patient with pityriasis alba.
Treat pityriasis alba conservatively by reducing sun exposure and recommending sunscreen and moisturizers. B

For significantly bothersome pityriasis alba not responding to conservative treatment, consider using topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment twice daily for 9 weeks to decrease hypopigmentation and scaling. B
Topical steroids have not been studied for pityriasis alba, but have been recommended based on the epidemiologic and histopathologic association of pityriasis alba and atopic dermatitis. C
Topical steroids have not been studied for pityriasis alba, but have been recommended based on the epidemiologic and histopathologic association of pityriasis alba and atopic dermatitis.

In an open-label randomized placebo-controlled study of 60 patients between the ages of 6 and 21 years with pityriasis alba and phototype III-IV, tacrolimus 0.1% ointment twice daily for 9 weeks decreased hypopigmentation and scaling more than moisturizer and sunscreen alone. Twelve percent of patients reported a mild, transient burning sensation with the application of tacrolimus. All of the patients (100%) in the tacrolimus group were either satisfied or completely satisfied with the treatment compared with 50% in the moisturizer/sunscreen group.

A small, single-arm study of 10 patients (ages 12-35) with pityriasis alba who appiled 1% pimecrolimus twice per day for 12 weeks showed a reduction in scaling and uneven skin color without any adverse effects. While this study is significantly limited, pimecrolimus may be an alternative option for the treatment of pityriasis alba.
Reassure patients and families that pityriasis alba is a common, benign, and self-limited condition.
Reduce sun exposure.
Use moisturizers regularly.
Use sunscreen daily. Half of children with pityriasis alba treated with moisturizer and sunscreen twice a day for 9 weeks were satisfied/completely satisfied with the treatment.
Reduce bathing to once a day or less.
Use lukewarm (rather than hot) water in baths.

Laser phototherapy with a 308-nm excimer laser may be an effective treatment modality. A small study with 12 patients showed improvement in scaling, hypopigmentation, and pruritis after 12 weeks with no significant adverse effects.

No follow-up is needed, unless the family has additional concerns or the patient is being treated with medication. C
